title: Deadlocks
relevance: Tests whether candidates can reason about concurrent resource waits, the Coffman conditions, and Banker's-style safety analysis common in SDE interviews and OAs.
company_notes: Cisco-style Banker's questions often grant a process request before testing whether an ordering is a safe sequence; Linux and Windows typically use deadlock ignorance (the Ostrich algorithm).

phases.goal: Establish what deadlock is, the four Coffman conditions, and how it differs from starvation and livelock.

must_hit.point: Deadlock is a permanent circular block: a set of processes each waits for a resource another in the set holds, so the awaited release never happens.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States permanent blocking with mutual wait for held resources, not just temporary delay.

must_hit.point: All four Coffman conditions must hold at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait; breaking any one makes deadlock impossible.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all four by name and says they are necessary and jointly sufficient for deadlock to be possible.

must_hit.point: Deadlock, starvation, and livelock are distinct: starvation is indefinite denial of a runnable process; livelock is active state change with no progress.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts permanent circular block vs indefinitely denied progress vs busy no-progress interaction.

probes: What is a deadlock, and what four conditions are required for one to occur?
How is deadlock different from starvation and livelock?

hints.1: Think about processes stuck waiting on each other for resources.
hints.2: Name the four Coffman conditions and say why each is needed.
hints.3: Deadlock = permanent circular wait; starvation = indefinitely denied; livelock = changing state but never finishing.

phases.goal: Show how resource-allocation graphs and the Banker's safety algorithm decide whether a state is deadlocked or safe.

must_hit.point: With single-instance resources, a cycle in the RAG is necessary and sufficient for deadlock.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says cycle means deadlock and no cycle means no deadlock when each type has one instance.

must_hit.point: With multiple-instance resources, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient; the graph alone is inconclusive and the detection/safety algorithm on allocation and request matrices is required.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains another holder may release an instance and break the wait, so you must run the matrix algorithm.

must_hit.point: Avoidance keeps a safe state: there exists a safe sequence where each process can obtain its maximum needs using Available plus resources freed earlier; Need = Max − Allocation; grant a request only if the resulting state stays safe.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines safe sequence, Need as Max minus Allocation, and refusal to enter an unsafe state.

must_hit.point: The safety algorithm repeatedly finds a process with Need ≤ Available, pretends it finishes, and returns its allocation to Available; if all finish, the state is safe.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the iterative Need ≤ Available check and releasing allocation back into Available.

probes: When does a cycle in a resource-allocation graph imply deadlock?
Walk through how the Banker's safety algorithm decides whether a state is safe.

hints.1: Separate the single-instance RAG rule from the multiple-instance case.
hints.2: For Banker's, start from Available and look for Need ≤ Available processes in order.
hints.3: Single-instance: cycle iff deadlock; multi-instance: cycle only a warning; safety = finish everyone by Need ≤ Available then reclaim.

phases.goal: Contrast the four deadlock-handling strategies and the costs of breaking each Coffman condition.

must_hit.point: Four strategies exist: ignorance (Ostrich—reboot if hung; used by most general-purpose OSes because prevention cost is not worth paying continuously), prevention, avoidance with advance maximum claims (Banker's), and detection plus recovery.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all four strategies and notes ignorance as the common OS choice for rarity vs continuous cost.

must_hit.point: Prevention costs: shareable resources are not always possible; request-all-up-front lowers utilization and risks starvation; preemption works only for saveable state (CPU, memory), not printers; global resource ordering is the most practical rule.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps each Coffman break to its downside and calls global ordering the most practical.

must_hit.point: Detection recovers by process termination (all at once or one-by-one by priority/progress/resources held) or resource preemption with rollback, which can starve a repeatedly chosen victim.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions aborting deadlocked processes and preempting resources with checkpoint rollback and starvation risk.

probes: Compare deadlock ignorance, prevention, avoidance, and detection/recovery—when would you choose each?
What are the practical costs of breaking each of the four Coffman conditions?

hints.1: List the four handling strategies from doing nothing to detect-and-recover.
hints.2: For each Coffman condition, say how prevention breaks it and what you give up.
hints.3: Ostrich for rare deadlocks; prevention via ordering is most practical in code; Banker's needs max claims; detection then abort or preempt.

phases.goal: Apply lock ordering, safe-sequence simulation, and the deadlock-free resource-count bound to concrete cases.

must_hit.point: Breaking circular wait with a global resource ordering carries into code: always acquire locks in the same fixed order so cyclic wait—and deadlock—becomes impossible.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States fixed lock-acquire order as the coding discipline that prevents circular wait.

must_hit.point: Checking whether an ordering is a safe sequence is a simulation: walk left to right, require Need ≤ current Available at each step, then add that process's allocation back; it is unsafe the moment some Need exceeds Available.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes walking Available through the given order, not using a closed formula.

must_hit.point: For n processes with maxima d_i on one resource type, deadlock-free requires R ≥ sum(d_i − 1) + 1 = sum d_i − n + 1; when every maximum is k, R ≥ n(k − 1) + 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the worst-case hold d_i−1 each, then +1 frees progress, and the equal-k reduction.

must_hit.point: In the worked Banker's example with totals A=10, B=5, C=7 and Available ⟨3,3,2⟩, one safe sequence is ⟨P2, P4, P5, P1, P3⟩; any sequence that starts with P1 is not safe because Need ⟨7,4,3⟩ exceeds initial Available ⟨3,3,2⟩.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites Available ⟨3,3,2⟩, the safe sequence starting P2, and why starting with P1 fails.

probes: Why does acquiring locks in a fixed global order prevent deadlock?
Given Available and Need vectors, how do you tell whether a candidate ordering is a safe sequence?
Three processes each need at most 2 units of one resource; what is the minimum R that guarantees no deadlock?

hints.1: Connect circular-wait prevention to how you order lock acquires in code.
hints.2: For safety checks, simulate Available forward; for resource counts, use each process holding d_i−1.
hints.3: Fixed lock order kills cycles; walk Need ≤ Available; for n=3 and d_i=2, R ≥ 3(2−1)+1 = 4.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Ignorance (Ostrich) pretends deadlocks never happen and reboots if the system hangs; most general-purpose OSes choose this because deadlocks are rare and continuous prevention cost is not worth paying. Prevention designs out a Coffman condition; avoidance allows the conditions but refuses unsafe grants using maximum claims (Banker's); detection lets deadlocks occur then recovers by abort or preemption.

tradeoffs.topic: Breaking hold-and-wait vs breaking circular wait
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Requesting all resources up front eliminates hold-and-wait but yields low utilization and starvation risk. Imposing a global ordering on resource types so processes only request in increasing order breaks circular wait and is the most practical prevention rule, matching real lock-ordering disciplines.

tradeoffs.topic: Process termination vs resource preemption for recovery
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Termination aborts all deadlocked processes or aborts one at a time until the cycle breaks, choosing victims by priority, progress, or resources held. Preemption takes a resource, rolls the victim back to a checkpoint, and risks starvation if the same process is always chosen.

gotchas.trap: Treating deadlock, starvation, and livelock as the same failure mode.
gotchas.correction: Deadlock is a permanent circular block; starvation is a process that could run being indefinitely denied a resource; livelock is processes actively changing state in response to each other yet making no progress.

gotchas.trap: Assuming any cycle in a resource-allocation graph means deadlock.
gotchas.correction: That holds only for single-instance resources. With multiple instances, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient—another process may release an instance in the cycle—so you must run the detection/safety algorithm.

gotchas.trap: Treating an unsafe state as already deadlocked.
gotchas.correction: An unsafe state is not necessarily deadlocked; it may lead to deadlock, so avoidance refuses to enter it.

gotchas.trap: Answering 'is X a safe sequence?' with a formula instead of simulation.
gotchas.correction: Run the Available vector forward through the ordering, checking Need ≤ Available at each process. If a fresh request is granted first, subtract it from Available and add it to that process's allocation before walking.

gotchas.trap: Confusing the deadlock-possible bound with the deadlock-free bound on resource count.
gotchas.correction: Deadlock is possible when R ≤ sum d_i − n; deadlock-free when R ≥ sum(d_i − 1) + 1 = sum d_i − n + 1 (or R ≥ n(k−1)+1 when every maximum is k).
